info.bio: William "Smokey" Robinson, Jr. (born February 19, 1940) is an American R&B and soul singer and songwriter. Robinson is noted for being one of the primary figures associated with the Motown record label, second only to the company's founder, Berry Gordy. As both a member of Motown group The Miracles and a solo artist, Robinson recorded seventy Top 40 hits for Motown between 1959 and 1990, and also served as the company's Vice President from 1961 to 1988.

scenes.name: Soul y R&B
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El 1 de enero de 1966 el Top 3 estadounidense lo formaban «The Sound of Silence», «We Can Work It Out» y el «I Got You (I Feel Good)» de James Brown: discos futuristas los tres. A finales de mes Otis Redding se acercaba al Top 10 británico con su versión de «My Girl» de los Temptations.

scenes.name: Motown: Supremes y Holland-Dozier-Holland
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Los grupos de Tamla/Motown ocuparon el hueco de los girl groups: Martha and the Vandellas («Heat Wave», «Dancing in the Street», «Nowhere to Run»), Gladys Knight, las Marvelettes, las Velvelettes y, sobre todo, las Supremes, el grupo pop americano de más éxito del momento (seis números 1 en dos años). Tres amigas del proyecto Brewster-Douglass, las «Supremes sin éxitos» hasta «Where Did Our Love Go» (1964): Berry Gordy vio en ellas el caballo de Troya para entrar en el mercado blanco, con los Funk Brothers, la escritura «psicológica» de Holland-Dozier-Holland (playlets femeninos sobre el amor como adicción, música dura contra letras sumisas) y el departamento de Artist Development de Maxine Powell y Cholly Atkins. Su imagen de espectáculo (Copacabana, pelucas) contrastaba con la nueva bohemia rock, como en su incómodo encuentro con unos Beatles fumados. Diana Ross ardía: seis números 1 y aún las trataban como a un grupo cualquiera.

scenes.name: Motown, Norman Whitfield y la psicodelia soul
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: El imperio de Berry Gordy fue un fenómeno de capitalismo negro, pero en los setenta solo sobrevivieron los artistas que escribían su material (Stevie Wonder, Marvin Gaye, Smokey Robinson, Michael Jackson). Norman Whitfield, que pasó de chupatintas a productor, le dio un filo más áspero («I Heard It Through the Grapevine» de Gladys Knight) y, mientras Sly arrasaba en 1968, cambió el sonido de los Temptations: temas largos con guitarras rockeras, efectos espaciales, drogas («Cloud Nine», «Psychedelic Shack», «Ball of Confusion») y orgullo negro, ropa a lo Hendrix y, al final, «Papa Was a Rollin’ Stone» (1972), soul con mensaje. La huella de P-Funk era clara (Eddie Hazel y Billy Nelson tocan en «Shakey Ground»); Whitfield convirtió a los Undisputed Truth en una banda de black rock pintada de plata. Los músicos de sesión, los Funk Brothers, trabajaban en la sombra: el bajista James Jamerson, que sacaba líneas de cómo hablaba o caminaba la gente, influyó a todos. Cuando Motown se mudó a Los Ángeles, la banda se quedó en Detroit y la magia se perdió.

scenes.name: Ska jamaicano y soul de los sesenta
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: El ska, «R&B dado vuelta», nace a finales de los cincuenta; Prince Buster, su supuesto inventor, era aún más conocido en Inglaterra, donde los mods lo escoltaban en motoneta. Los mods originales que no se pasaron a la psicodelia se hicieron skinheads amantes del ska y el rocksteady o fans del Motown y el northern soul («a mí me gusta la música para bailar, no escuchar»). Geno Washington y su Ram Jam Band, el soul de Stax y Atlantic: el repertorio que 2-Tone y Dexys recuperan.

scenes.name: Soul y Motown
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Al otro lado del océano, la alternativa a los grupos británicos fue el heredero del rhythm'n'blues: el soul. El sonido Memphis (Wilson Pickett, Otis Redding, Sam & Dave) nace de bandas instrumentales casi anónimas como Booker T & the MG's; Motown triunfa con el soul melódico y bailable de Stevie Wonder, Smokey Robinson y el trío Holland-Dozier-Holland («quizá el mayor fenómeno pop de todos los tiempos»); Phil Spector lanza el «blue-eyed soul» con los Righteous Brothers, y James Brown, con su estilo percusivo, inventa el funk.
scenes.family: Soul, funk, disco, hip hop y baile

scenes.name: Motown, P-Funk y el funk del Medio Oeste
scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
scenes.author: Dan Sicko
scenes.desc: El legado del que los jóvenes del techno querían escapar y que, sin saberlo, llevaban dentro. Detroit lo había tenido todo (el blues urbano de John Lee Hooker, el jazz de Elvin Jones y Milt Jackson, el gospel, MC5, Bob Seger y la cadena de montaje de Motown), pero Berry Gordy se llevó Motown en 1972 y la ciudad se quedó sin red cultural, sin la voz de Marvin Gaye y Smokey Robinson. El funk de George Clinton, Zapp y los Ohio Players, el R&B electrónico de Shannon y el soul de Motown se mezclan, a veces de forma inconsciente, en los primeros discos electrónicos de Detroit.

podcast.title: Eternally Youthful (1987)
podcast.body: Smokey Robinson was described as "eternally youthful" and scored some hits in 1987, making him one of the few artists alongside Aretha Franklin at the time who was a current hitmaker among Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductees, though he did not have a new number one hit. "other than the eternally youthful Smokey Robinson, who would score some hits in 87. I would do anything. None of the other Rock Hall nominees that night could make that claim. And even Smokey didn't have a new number one hit."

podcast.title: Primary Producer for The Marvelettes
podcast.body: After "Please Mr. Postman," Smokey Robinson became the primary writer and producer for many of The Marvelettes' records, and later took over their production entirely, strategically shifting lead vocals to Wonder Young. "But while those records did okay on the R&B chart, they didn't have much success on the pop charts, mostly getting to around number 50. At one point Motown started to wonder if they needed to change things up a little. They put out a single by the group with Gladys and Wonder singing a dual lead, and with the group joined by Motown's in-house backing vocal group The Andantees. The record was put out under the name The Darnells, but was unsuccessful. Unfortunately for them, they missed the chance at a really big hit. Holland, Doge and Holland had written a song for them, but Gladys didn't like it. She thought it was too simplistic, and so they took it to the group who were still known with him Motown as the no-hit Supremes. We'll be looking at Where Did I Love Go in more detail next year. Eddie Holland did co-writer hit for them with Norman Whitfield though, though it wasn't a monster hit like Where Did I Love Go. It did give all the girls a chance to have a solo spot, a rarity for them. They took them back into the top 30 and made the top 5 on the R&B chart. It would be the last hit that they would have with George Anna in the group though. She'd been diagnosed with sickle cell anemia as a child, and the constant strain of touring made her more ill. The tours had been a shock for all of them to be honest. Their first major national tour was the first Motown review in 1962, a tour with a lineup that seems preposterously good these days. All of Motown's major acts and several acts that weren't yet major but soon would be were on the same bill. The miracles, Marywells, the Marvillette, the Temptations, Marv Johnson, Stevie Wonder, the Contours, Marvin Gaye, Martha and the Vandellas, the Supremes and singing Samry Ward."

podcast.title: Responding to Barry Gordy's 3 AM Call
podcast.body: Smokey Robinson was called by Barry Gordy at 3 AM to quickly gather The Miracles and re-record "Shop Around" with a faster arrangement. This urgent session led to the song becoming a massive hit, showcasing Robinson's dedication and responsiveness. "He'd phoned up Smokey and told him to get the group together and into the studio, before he lost the inspiration, even though it was the middle of the night."
